pages.title: Squatting in Venezuela
pages.text:
Squatting in Venezuela is the occupation of derelict buildings or unused land without the permission of the owner. Informal settlements, known first as "ranchos" and then "barrios", are common. In the capital Caracas notable squats have included the 23 de Enero housing estate, Centro Financiero Confinanzas (a derelict skyscraper) and El Helicoide, a former shopping centre which is now a notorious prison.


== History ==
Following the 1948 Venezuelan coup d'état, the military junta followed a process of shanty town eradication and forcible resettlement. The informal settlements were known as ranchos, and shacks were built out of recycled materials such as cinder blocks, metal, cardboard and cement.


== 23 de Enero superblocks ==

Following the 1958 Venezuelan coup d'état, thousands of people occupied empty apartments in the superblocks of the 2 de Diciembre (2 December) housing estate, which had been built in tribute to the then President of Venezuela, Marcos Pérez Jiménez. After he had been deposed, the new residents renamed the 37 blocks to 23 de Enero (23 January), marking the date of the coup.
At the time of the coup, there were 47,000 people living in the blocks and some had been forcibly resettled there. The population then exploded to 72,000 overnight. The authorities struggled to regularize the new residents and to collect rent, which in some cases the squatters were reluctant to pay since the apartments were unfinished and there were problems with the water supply. As well as the new occupiers of the buildings, between 20,000 and 25,000 people created new ranchos in the area of 23 de Enero. Some renters then decided it was more cost-effective to live in a shack and left their apartments. Squatters who had occupied the local schools were also relocated. Whilst the state tolerated the block squatters, it decided to evict the ranchos, in a policy reminiscent of the previous dictatorship. The artist Feliciano Carvallo was given two days notice to move and then his rancho was burnt down and he lost 20 paintings. By 1959, there were still 15,000 ranchos at 23 de Enero.


== Recent ==
In 1989, the Caracazo resulted in the deaths of many inhabitants of informal settlements, now commonly known as "barrios". In consequence, the Asamblea de Barrios was formed to campaign for the rights of shanty town dwellers. This then joined the Bolivaran movement which resulted in Hugo Chávez becoming the president in December 1998. At this time, nine of ten Venezuelans lived in urban areas and over half were squatters. Chávez introduced a program in 2002 which was run by the National Technical Office for the Regularization of Urban Land Tenancy and aimed to give rancho dwellers title to their land. The state planned to build 3 million houses by 2019, under Mission Habitat and Great Mission Housing Venezuela.
The Centro Financiero Confinanzas is an unfinished skyscraper that became a notorious symbol of the Venezuelan banking crisis of 1994. After years of dereliction, it was squatted in 2007 by evangelical Christians as part of a wave of occupations in Caracas. Around 3,000 people lived there before being resettled in 2014. An earlier squatted building in Caracas was El Helicoide, which is located in the barrio of San Agustín del Sur. Intended to be a shopping centre it was never completed then occupied by 10,000 people between 1979 and 1982, some of whom had been previously displaced by its construction. The Bolivarian Intelligence Service took over the building in 1985 and it has become a notorious prison, where people participating in the ongoing protests have been taken to be tortured. In the 2020 World Justice Project Rule of Law Index, Venezuela was rated 128th out 128 countries.

pages.title: Alcaldes del cambio
pages.text:
Alcaldes del cambio (Spanish for Mayors of change) is the name given to a group of local elected politicians after the 2015 municipal elections in Spain, following the 2008 financial crisis and the anti-austerity protests that formed the 15-M movement.
These mayors reached power by defeating the traditional parties of Spanish politics: the centre-left Spanish Socialist Workers' Party and mostly the conservative People's Party, who in cities such as Madrid, Valencia or Cádiz had been governing for over two decades. Most of their platforms were formed as municipalist-centered citizen movements supported by newer left-wing parties like Podemos or more established forces such as Izquierda Unida, as well as local grassroots organizations. Despite their anti-establishment rhetoric against the traditional two-party system (known as bipartidismo), most of them did not win outright majorities in their local assemblies and instead had to rely on parliamentary backing from other parties, particularly from the PSOE, to successfully oust the incumbent administrations.
Among their proposals, under the label of "new politics", they promised to fight against corruption and austerity, improving social policies such as housing or fighting child poverty, banning evictions or put a stop to real-estate bubble; green policies and advancing in direct democracy.


== Key policies ==

During their terms, these administrations implemented several structural changes in city management. Cities like Madrid, Barcelona, Cádiz or Zaragoza significantly reduced municipal public debt while increasing social spending. Barcelona and Valencia pioneered sustainable urban models, notably through the creation of Barcelona's Superblocks (Superilles) and the massive expansion of Valencia's bicycle lane infrastructure under Ribó. In Madrid, Carmena's administration promoted the so-called "renaturalización del Manzanares" (renaturalization), whilst Ribó in Valencia attempted to do the same within the old Turia river basin that crosses through the city. In Zaragoza, Santisteve increased the city council's spending in public housing and created superblocks following the Barcelona model.
Several cities attempted to remunicipalize public services, such as water supply, funeral services, or garbage collection, with varying degrees of administrative success, as well as the pedestrianization of their city centres.


== Controversies and criticisms ==
Despite their focus on social justice and transparency, these administrations faced significant opposition and polarization throughout their terms, including tourism and commercial friction, accusations of "alleged permissiveness" regarding unregulated street vending (known as manteros) and illegal housing squats (okupas) leading to intense media debates over public safety and urban order; intense backlash from motorist associations, transport lobbies and merchant unions over major infrastructure shifts such as the implementation of Madrid Central under Carmena or the massive expansion of bicycle lanes and pedestrian zones in Valencia, whose restrictions they claimed the restrictions harmed commerce; or the fact that these administrations operated under severe financial constraints imposed by the national government's Budgetary Stability Law of 2012 (popularly known as the Montoro Law), which forced municipalities to prioritize debt repayment over local investments. In late 2017, this led to a major political crisis within Madrid's government, culminating in Carmena dismissing her own economic councilor, Carlos Sánchez Mato, to avoid a direct intervention of the city's accounts by the national Ministry of Finance.


== List ==


== Decline and legacy ==
The "mayors of change" era faced a sharp decline starting in 2019 due to internal fragmentation within the left-wing coalitions (notably the split between Podemos and Más Madrid), intense media opposition and judicial challenges against municipal decrees, with heavy judicialization of municipal governance. Left-wing platforms frequently denounced what they described as a coordinated campaign of "lawfare".
Dozens of criminal complaints and lawsuits were filed against mayors and city councilors by investment funds, real-estate lobbies, and far-right legal organizations such as Manos Limpias. These lawsuits targeted municipal housing policies, green zone regulations and public service remunicipalization projects. While the vast majority of these criminal cases were ultimately archived and dismissed by Spanish judges due to a lack of evidence of wrongdoing, the constant legal challenges created significant administrative delays and sustained negative media coverage throughout their mandates.
In the 2019 municipal elections, platforms in Madrid, Zaragoza, Santiago, Ferrol and La Coruña lost power to right-wing coalitions. José María González "Kichi" in Cádiz, Ada Colau in Barcelona, and Joan Ribó in Valencia managed to secure second terms. However, González chose not to run again in 2023, and both Colau and Ribó lost their mayoralties following the May 2023 municipal elections, effectively bringing an end to the political phenomenon.


=== Legacy ===
In Madrid, Manuela Carmena pedestrianized the Gran Vía, implemented a low-emission zone (Madrid Central) and promoted a reform in the area surrounding the Temple of Debod, the Plaza de España square and Príncipe Pío along with the renaturalization of the Manzanares area known as Madrid Río and the decision to cover the new section of the city where the estadio Vicente Calderón instead of placing it underground. Despite initial opposition from his eventual successor José Luis Martínez-Almeida to most or all of these reforms, he decided to keep or modify some of them instead of scrapping them.
In Valencia, Ribó implemented many cycling lanes throughout the city, whilst his successor María José Catalá promised to dismantle.
